Thrombi are typically mobile within the bladder and will organize and contract with time. Changing patient body position to assess for movement within the lumen and serial monitoring for changes in appearance may be helpful. Use of color flow Doppler can generally differentiate between neoplasia and thrombi based on the presence or absence of blood flow within the structure. Neoplasia will have blood flow and thrombi will not (neither will artifact). Thrombi may be iatrogenic and associated with a recent history of cystocentesis. Regardless of etiology, these should shrink and resolve with time, whereas neoplasia will typically progress over time (see Figure 11.11). In the dog, the most common location of TCC is near the trigone (Leveille et al. 1992) but they can occur in any region of the bladder wall or urethra, and can occasionally be seen extending into the urethra from the bladder lumen or into the bladder lumen from the urethra. TCC is more common in females. Obstruction of the ureters with secondary hydronephrosis may occur due to obstruction of the ureteral papillae by tumor. Therefore, assessment of the ureters and kid - neys is indicated, and easily performed for further evaluation of the urinary tract in patients with sus - pected TCC. In fact, the Global FAST approach allows for rapid same‐day staging for obvious hydronephro - sis, liver, and pulmonary metastasis as well as any cardiac complications (see Chapters 10 and XX). In cats, TCC is less common than in dogs and more often seen in older males. Although extremely rare, TCC has the potential to seed along the needle track, resulting in regional spread of the tumor (Nyland et al. 2002; Vignoli et al. 2007; Liffman and Courtman 2017). Ultrasound‐guided suction biopsy of the mass by urinary catheter may provide ample cells or tissue for diagnosis. Referral for a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound by an experienced sonographer is recommended if fine needle aspirates are to be pursued. Intraluminal Abnormalities Intraluminal abnormalities of the urinary bladder include calculi, blood clots (thrombi), and sediment. Calculi (Bladder Stones) Calculi (bladder stones) are discrete mobile objects with curvilinear hyperechoic (bright) surfaces within the lumen of the bladder. They are generally round in appearance but may be variable in shape and size, and may be clustered together. Calculi usually have a distal acoustic shadow but very small calculi (<1–2 mm) may not produce an appreciable shadow (Figure 11.8). However, in people, a new artifact, referred to as the “twinkle artifact,” has been used to detect uroliths (renal, ureteral, and bladder) that are <5 mm, a tradi- tionally difficult size range to accurately diagnose with B‐mode (Gliga et al. 2017). This twinkle artifact, cre- ated by intrinsic ultrasound machine noise seen with color flow Doppler, has been shown to be more sensitive for the detection of small stones (<5 mm) than acoustic shadowing. The twinkle artifact is most apparent when the reflecting surface of the urolith (renal, ureteral, or cystic) is irregular and the focal zone is placed below the reflecting surface of the suspect object. In summary, the twinkle artifact occurs when color flow Doppler is applied to the region (suspect stone) in question and red/blue turbulent or pulse‐like “twinkling” is seen behind the mineralization (Gliga et al. 2017). Interestingly, the twinkle artifact may be applied to other organs with suspected mineralization (Gliga et al. 2017). Size of the calculi is important to note and record as it may have clinical implications regarding therapy, particularly for evaluating the likelihood of a calculus safely passing through the urethra either spontane- ously or by voiding hydropropulsion. The following guidelines for voiding urohydropulsion (VUH) have been published (Defarges et al. 2013). • Female dogs (>2 kg) can typically void stones <3–4 mm. • Female cats may be able to void stones <3 mm. • Male dogs weighing 5–10 kg may be able to void stones <2–3 mm; male dogs >10 kg may be able to void stones <3 mm. • Male cats: voiding urohydropulsion is not recommended. The number of calculi is also important to assess, although cannot often be accurately established, par - ticularly when calculi are clustered together. Note also that calculi may be located within the urethra, and the proximal and prostatic urethra should be visualized for intraluminal calculi. Pearl: The ease of passing a 9 French urinary cath- eter correlates with the successful voiding of 3 mm stones. Pearl: The presence of echogenic urine is not specific for urinary tract infection or other pathology and a urinalysis (and urine culture) should be obtained to determine the significance of the ultrasonographic finding(s). Pitfall and Pearl: Gas, formed fecal matter in the colon, and associated artifacts (i.e., acoustic shadow) can mimic a urinary calculus when the bladder rests against the colon, and the bladder wall indents and curves to the contour of the fecal‐filled colon. While centering on the possible calculus, slide the transducer cranially. If the hyperechoic mass with the acoustic shadow can be followed cranial to the bladder, then it is not a calculus. Alternately, turn the transducer 90° and if the suspected item elongates into a tubular structure, then it is not a calculus (see Figure 11.3). Pearl: The “twinkle artifact” is a recently described effective technique (>90% sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values) to detect small calculi and mineralization of <5 mm in the urinary tract from the kidney to the urinary bladder through the use of color flow Doppler. The tech- nique may in fact be applied to any organ with sus- pect mineralization (Gliga et al. 2017). Pearl: Calculi can be assessed for mobility within the lumen by agitating the bladder (ballottement) with the transducer or by changing patient body position. It will produce an acoustic shadow when mineralized (i.e., crystals, sand, tiny calculi). Agitation of the bladder (ballottement) is recommended in all urinary bladder interrogations and may result in suspension and swirling of the sediment or the so‐called “snow globe” appearance. Repositioning the patient can also result in movement of the sediment to the gravity‐ dependent surface (see repositioning for cystic calculi above). A urinalysis should be performed to evaluate the significance and composition of sediment seen on ultrasound examination (Figures 11.9 and 11.10; see also Figure 11.8B). AFAST improves the diagnostic potential of the ultrasound examination by detecting peritoneal effusion. 246: 223 POCUS: URINARY BLADDER Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • The urinary bladder is generally easy to evaluate for obvious intraluminal (e.g., calculi or blood clots) and mural (e.g., mass lesions) abnormalities. • Moderate distension of the urinary bladder is necessary for optimal assessment for urinary bladder wall thickness and the presence of focal wall abnormalities. An empty urinary bladder can often be misinterpreted as having a thickened urinary bladder wall. • When evaluating for diffuse changes, cystitis gen- erally results in hypoechoic thickening, most often along the cranioventral or apical aspect of the urinary bladder. • Severe or polypoid cystitis is not distinguishable from diffuse mural urinary bladder neoplasia. If ultrasonographic changes persist or worsen dur - ing/following medical therapy for cystitis, tissue sampling should be pursued. However, the add‐on of a Global FAST rapidly screens for localized versus disseminated disease and should be used the same day for staging the patient. • Ureteral papillae occasionally may be seen on the dorsal surface of the bladder wall near the trigone and should not be confused with a urinary bladder wall abnormality. • The contents of the colon can cause shadowing artifacts that may be mistaken for calculi or sedi- ment and moving the patient to a standing position will help discriminate artifact from true abnormal- ities. Unless adhered, uroliths and sediment will fall to the gravity‐dependent location (artifact will not) and pressure impingement from the colon along the ventral urinary bladder surface will be relieved. • The ultrasonographic interrogation of the urinary bladder is susceptible to many artifacts, which may lead to misinterpretation. Therefore, it is impera- tive to be familiar with these artifacts and how to mitigate them as with interrogating the urinary bladder from multiple vantage points or changing patient position in order to provide an accurate assessment of the findings and paying attention to gravity‐dependent regions where sediment, cal- culi, and blood clots would settle. • Blood clots (thrombi) may be variable in echo- genicity and may be difficult to distinguish from bladder wall masses, especially if they are adhered to the wall. Use color flow Doppler to help differ - entiate them as neoplasia generally has positive (blood) flow and blood clots and artifacts do not. • Additional diagnostic techniques may be needed following the POCUS urinary bladder examination to further define disorders of the lower urinary tract. This may include referral for a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound by an experienced sonographer and/or additional perineal radiog- raphy in the male patient for urethral evaluation, special radiographic studies or computed tomo- graphic imaging of the entire urinary tract, which are especially helpful in further assessing the kid- neys, ureters, urethra, and pelvic inlet. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • The thickness of the urinary bladder wall varies depending on the degree of distension. • Normal range for urinary bladder wall thickness is cats 1.3–1.7 mm (Finn‐Bodner 1995). • Normal ranges for urinary bladder wall thickness in dogs are from 1.4 mm in moderately distended bladders to 2.3 mm in minimally distended blad- ders (Geisse et al. 1997). However, wall thickness in dogs has been reported to increase with body size, with heavier dogs having increased thickness by up to 1 mm or a maximum normal thickness of ≤3 mm (Geisse et al. 1997). • The urinary bladder, being fluid filled, is subject to several artifacts including side‐lobe, edge shadow- ing, and acoustic enhancement in the far‐field. • Voiding urohydropulsion guidelines are as follows. ◦ Female dogs (>2 kg) can typically void stones <3–4 mm. ◦ Female cats may be able to void stones <3 mm. ◦ Male dogs weighing 5–10 kg may be able to void stones <2–3 mm; male dogs >10 kg may be able to void stones <3 mm. ◦ Male cats: VUH is not recommended. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 225 Introduction Typically, a point‐of‐care ultrasound (POCUS) examina- tion is not extensive, thorough or complete. Rather, it provides a limited examination designed to answer brief and important clinical questions in an organ system or for a symptom involving multiple organ sys- tems (Mateer et al. 1994). In the emergency setting, it can provide early diagnostic information that can guide treatment of the critical patient. This is especially true in situations where delaying ultrasonographic evaluation until a specialist is available, or positioning the patient for complete ultrasonographic evaluation or radiog- raphy, might lead to further patient compromise. Some gastrointestinal (GI)‐related conditions that have been evaluated with emergency ultrasound in people include intussusception, small bowel obstruc- tion, pyloric stenosis, appendicitis, gastric ulcers, per - forated hollow viscus, gallbladder rupture, septic peritonitis, acute mesenteric ischemia, and acute pan- creatitis (Rozycki 2001; Dean et al. 2002; Unluer et al. 2010; Testa et al. 2010; Jang et al. 2011). Using the AFAST examination technique to evaluate for the presence of peritoneal fluid has been validated in dogs (Boysen et al. 2004; Lisciandro et al. 2009) and whether or not peritonitis exists is an important clinical question to answer. However, a more detailed approach to scanning of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and pancreatic pathologies requires considerably more expertise and training, which may limit the use of POCUS GIT and pancreas by some emergency clini- cians. It must be stressed that POCUS GIT and pan- creas should not replace abdominal radiographs, complete detailed abdominal ultrasound or computed tomography (CT) examination for a more compre- hensive peritoneal cavity evaluation. Furthermore, in people the correlation obtained between emergency physician POCUS and a gold standard pathology confirmation varies by operator experience and the extent and type of training received for the above‐ mentioned GI conditions (Raymond‐Dufresne and Ghanayem 2012; Hasani et al. 2015). This emphasizes the potential advantages and limitations of POCUS GIT and pancreas emergency examination in the acute GI setting. However, abnormal ultrasonographic findings (a positive result) can be extremely valuable in providing a diagnosis and guiding initial case management. A negative emergency POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nation is not uncommon and does not necessarily rule out disease (false negative) indicating the need for further diagnostic testing, serial POCUS GIT and pan- creas plus AFAST, or follow‐up with an imaging spe- cialist. In other words, POCUS GIT and pancreas should be considered a rule‐in test for organ pathology. On the other hand, AFAST for intraabdominal fluid detection, evidence for peritonitis, is both a rule‐in (highly specific) and rule‐out (highly sensitive) test for the nonradiologist sonographer (Boysen et al. 2004). For the sonographer who is not confident in assigning the GIT or pancreas with a pathological sonographic diagnosis in acute abdomen cases, AFAST remains a very good screening test for peritonitis, a POCUS GIT and pancreas‐related consideration that warrants a prompt diagnosis. No studies exist evaluating the efficiency, accuracy, sensitivity or specificity of equivalent POCUS emergency GI ultrasound when performed by POCUS: Gastrointestinal Tract and Pancreas Søren R. However, evidence suggests that the diagnostic accuracy of detecting small intestinal mechanical obstruction in dogs using ultrasound is lower when performed by a novice sonographer compared to a boarded radiologist and that the learning curve is steeper for ultrasono- graphic GI assessment than for many other emergency POCUS techniques (Sharma et al. 2011). Currently, there are no standardized guidelines or recommenda- tions in the veterinary literature for performing POCUS emergency GI examinations. The accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of our POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nation have not been evaluated. We propose that POCUS GIT and pancreas be adapted and/or tailored to the critical patient and that, in many cases, it will provide valuable diagnostic information to better direct resuscitation, screen post resuscitation, and better keep patients alive for gold standard testing and treatment. The specific application of POCUS emergency examinations of the GIT depends on patient status, history, physical examination findings, clinical suspi- cion, and operator experience. Whether or not POCUS emergency examination for suspected GIT and pancreatic disease is warranted should be dictated by the availability of an experienced sonographer or radi- ologist and the assessment of preliminary diagnostic tests and dependent on the clinical questions to be answered by the attending veterinarian. In summary, when negative, POCUS GIT and pan- creas should not be considered a definitive test in the assessment of patients with suspected acute GI condi- tions. Instead, the application should be used as an initial screening, ancillary test to supplement the his- tory, physical examination findings, and other prelimi- nary diagnostic screening tests given its potential ability to direct initial therapy and guide appropriate diag- nostic testing, especially when other imaging modalities might be detrimental to the patient’s critical status, such as in those patients with profound anemia or compli- cating respiratory distress. When combined with AFAST, life‐threatening peritonitis can be ruled in or out, and a Global FAST approach can screen for thoracic (TFAST), cardiac (TFAST), and pulmonary comorbidi- ties (Vet BLUE) (see Chapters 7, 18, 23, and 36). What POCUS Gastrointestinal T ract and Pancreas Can Do • Provide a preliminary evaluation of patients with GI signs or evidence of acute abdomen in an effort to answer a specific question when complete abdominal ultrasonography is not available. • Rapidly assess the unstable patient with GI signs in an effort to rule in (or out) significant diffuse peri- toneal effusion. • Complement radiographic findings in cases with GI signs. • Support the clinical suspicion of moderate GI and pancreatic pathology for further testing to obtain a definitive diagnosis (i.e., ultrasound‐guided fine needle tissue sampling). • Detect the presence of peritonitis through the add‐ on of AFAST in initial and serial evaluations, and be complemented by Global FAST for further assessment of the thorax, heart, lung, and volume status. What POCUS Gastrointestinal T ract and Pancreas Cannot Do • Cannot replace a complete abdominal ultrasound examination or abdominal radiographs. • Cannot rule out focal or specific causes of GI pathology (particularly pancreatitis) when results are negative. Indications Two key factors to consider for POCUS GIT and pan- creas examinations are what the emergency clinician suspects is the underlying cause for presentation, and the urgency of finding an answer to the question asked. The stable patient may benefit more from a complete abdominal ultrasound exam whereas the unstable patient presenting “after hours” with signs of acute abdomen/GI signs is considered the ideal candidate for the POCUS GIT and pancreas examination. The indications and type of POCUS GIT and pan- creas examination vary and depend on the operator’s level of experience and training, presenting complaint, preliminary minimum database bloodwork results, physical examination findings, and suspected underlying condition of the patient. The indications for POCUS GIT and pancreas (plus AFAST) examination in the veterinary patient with acute GI signs include the clinical suspicion of pancre- atitis, screening for peritoneal effusion that might sug- gest perforated intestines, septic or biliary peritonitis, right‐sided cardiac failure, hemo‐ or uroabdomen or an underlying neoplastic process. The peritoneal space, stomach, and small and large bowel are readily evalu- ated for supportive evidence of GI perforation such as effusion shadowing GI foreign bodies, bowel intussus- ception, intestinal obstruction, and evidence of ileus.
250: 227 POCUS: GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT AND P ANCREAS Although not the ideal screening test for pneumoperi- toneum, peritoneal gas may also be detected. Examples of scenarios where an emergency clinician has a specific question that could potentially be answered by POCUS GIT and pancreas examination include the following. • In a patients with an acute abdomen, vomiting and unexplained hypotension, it is reasonable to ask if the patient has peritoneal effusion, which could be indicative of GI perforation and septic peritonitis. In these patients, an emergent AFAST examination may be performed to evaluate for effusion and aid in ultrasound‐guided abdominocentesis to screen for cytological evidence of sepsis. • In patients with acute abdominal pain and vomit- ing that are negative for peritoneal effusion, the emergency clinician may ask if the patient has localized or indirect evidence supportive of GI perforation or if a shadowing intestinal foreign body is present. POCUS GIT and pancreas exami- nation of the intestines may then be perfomed and may lead to the discovery of an ultrasonographi- cally detectable foreign body or raise the index of suspicion of intestinal obstruction. Indirect evi- dence of obstruction, such as a severely dilated jejunum with luminal dilation measuring greater than 1.5 cm, may highlight the need for a more extensive and complete ultrasonographic evalua- tion, abdominal radiographs, upper GI series or exploratory surgery (Sharma et al. 2011). The his- tory, physical examination, and other ancillary tests should be correlated with, and supportive of, the findings. • If the emergency clinician is experienced with ultrasonographic evaluation of the pancreas and the patient is hypotensive with a history suggestive of pancreatitis (such as exposure to a high‐fat meal followed by vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain), then a POCUS GIT and pancreas examina- tion may be performed to evaluate for ultrasono- graphic evidence of pancreatitis. If criteria for acute pancreatitis are present (e.g., hyperechoic or hyperattenuating mesentery with parenchymal pancreatic hypoechogenicity and elicitable pain in response to probe pressure during pancreatic eval- uation), the emergency clinician can then institute preliminary supportive measures while consid- ering further diagnostic and therapeutic options. • In patients that have undergone GI surgery and are deteriorating, the clinician may ask if dehiscence, septic peritonitis or postoperative ileus is present and may elect to perform an AFAST examination which would aid in ultrasound‐guided abdomino- centesis if peritoneal effusion is present. • In the postoperative patient that is vomiting, anorexic or painful, it is reasonable to ask if the patient has functional ileus and perform a POCUS emergency GIT examination to assess GI motility. Although perioperative gas may obscure ultraso- nographic peritoneal evaluation, if postoperative functional ileus is present, the clinician should search for and try to correct the underlying cause while considering specific therapies directed at addressing ileus. These are only a few examples of specific POCUS GIT and pancreas examination applications designed to answer a specific question. Although many factors dic- tate the clinical value of an AFAST study (the experi- ence of the operator, patient’s presenting complaint, and physical examination findings), there are many other clinical situations in which a patient can benefit from POCUS GIT and pancreas examination. Objectives • To identify the location, size, and shape of normal and abnormal peritoneal structures. • To identify pathology warranting specific or emergent treatment, optimizing early diagnosis and outcome of intraperitoneal disease, particu- larly in the unstable patient. Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Peritoneal Effusion See Chapters 6 and 7 for information on patient posi- tioning to look for the presence of peritoneal effusion. Gastrointestinal Evaluation Depending on the comfort level of the patient and preference of the sonographer, the POCUS emergency examination of the intestines may be performed in dorsal, left or right lateral recumbency. The overall status of the patient, with a particular focus on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, should be determined to ensure patients are stable before placing them in dorsal recumbency. If there is any doubt regarding clinical status, the patient should have thoracic POCUS, such as TFAST and Vet BLUE,
251: 228 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER performed to screen for intrathoracic problems including pleural and pericardial effusion, cardiac and pulmonary conditions, and abnormal volume status that may pose patient risk before moving the patient into dorsal recumbency (see Chapters 18, 23, and 36). • Left lateral recumbency helps with visualization of the pylorus and duodenum while right lateral recumbency allows for evaluation of the fundus (Penninck 2008a). • Repositioning the patient may redistribute intestinal gas and fluid allowing for specific regional evaluation. • Ultrasound probes with a frequency of at least 7.5 MHz are recommended for bowel evaluation (Penninck 2008a; Garcia et al. 2011). Pancreas Pancreatic scanning is frequently performed in dorsal recumbency although left and right lateral recumbency may also be used (Nyland et al. 2002; Penninck 2008b). • For pancreatic evaluation, a 5–7.5 MHz or higher transducer is preferred as higher frequencies improve visualization of the pancreas (Nyland et al. 2002). • Avoid examining the pancreas under high output or gain settings as the increased reflectivity of the pancreatic region prevents visualization of abnor - malities and leads to both false‐negative and false‐ positive results (Nyland et al. 2002; Hecht and Henry 2007). Scanning Technique Intestinal T ract The detection of GI lesions may be challenging given the difficulty of consistently evaluating the entire intestinal tract. Many factors, including normal or abnormal gas accumulation in the GI tract and oper - ator skill, influence the success of identifying GI lesions. A consistent and systematic technique will minimize false‐negative results. We propose the following POCUS GIT with the probe in the longitudinal plane. • One common technique involves starting in the region of the pylorus/stomach on the right side of the patient just caudal to the ribs and fanning the probe from the right to the left of the patient, paying specific attention to the stomach (located caudal to the xiphoid and liver) on the first pass. • Slide the probe 1–2 cm caudally and fan toward the far left side of the patient. Then fan back across the abdomen from left to right while paying specific attention to the bowel loops. • Repeated fanning of the probe across the abdomen in this fashion with a zig‐zag (or grid‐like) pattern while moving caudally will aid evaluation. If stable enough, the patient may be repositioned in various recumbencies for redistribution of fluid and gas, while repeating the evaluation (Figure 12.1). • The intestines are orientated in many directions. The above described approach results in the evalu- ation of many sections of small intestine in mul- tiple planes (sagittal, transverse, and various oblique planes), which depends on the probe‐to‐ intestinal tract orientation. • Once completed, if no irregularities are seen, the pylorus and descending duodenum can be evalu- ated in greater detail by returning the probe to the right side of the patient, just caudal to the ribcage (or, depending on patient conformation, some- times between the last ribs). The body of the stomach may first be located and traced to the pylorus, and then the descending duodenum. • This is a good time to get a general and subjective impression of overall gastric and small bowel motility (see section on Ileus below). • If a specific area of pain, mass or foreign object is palpated on initial physical examination, specific attention should be paid to the area in longitudinal and transverse planes. • Abnormal findings in close proximity to the area of suspicion might include intestinal wall structure layering abnormalities, abnormal intestinal peri- stalsis, focal loculations of peritoneal fluid, seg- mental focal dilations of small bowel, plicated bowel, target‐like lesions or hyperattenuating/ hyperechoic fat or mesentery. • Suspicious areas of intestine should be followed both orad and aborad to allow a more detailed assessment of these areas. • If structures within the GI lumen are visible, they should be carefully examined for a hyperechoic reflective interface and the presence of acoustic shadowing. Pancreas There are several scanning techniques that may be used to identify the pancreas, but a preferred tech- nique for POCUS emergency evaluation has not been

One of the more commonly used techniques in dogs involves an initial search for the right lobe of the pancreas as the right lobe is more easily imaged than the body and left lobe. Furthermore, the right lobe is more frequently affected by acute pancreatitis in the dog (Nyland et al. 2002; Hecht and Henry 2007; Penninck 2008b) whereas a higher prevelance is seen within the left pancreatic limb in cats with combined chronic pancreatic and gastrointestinal disease (De Cock et al. 2007). We propose the following POCUS pancreas. • The ultrasound probe is placed over the right kidney in transverse orientation. • After identifying the right kidney, the probe is slowly fanned laterally and medially until the descending duodenum is identified in transverse orientation. • The probe is then oriented in the sagittal plane, demonstrating that the duodenum may be evaluated along its length medial to the right abdominal body wall. • The pancreas is triangular shaped, and iso‐ to slightly hypoechoic (darker than) to surround - ing mesenteric fat. It has an echogenic capsule and is found dorsomedial to the duodenum, directly ventral to the right kidney (Hecht and Henry 2007). • The pancreaticoduodenal vessels and pancreatic duct may be seen as round anechoic structures within the pancreas (compare Figures 12.2 and 12.3). Color flow Doppler evaluation, if available, provides differentiation between the structures (see Figure 12.3A,B). • The portal vein may be seen and can be a useful landmark. It lies left and dorsal‐left to the pancreas and is best evaluated from a right dorsal intercostal approach (Brinkman‐Furguson and Biller 2009). • In very large or deep‐chested dogs, it may be easier to evaluated the right limb of the pancreas 1 2 3 6 7 5 8 4 Figure 12.1. The pancreatic body is located between the right and left lobes of the pancreas in close proximity to the portal vein, dorsocaudal to the pylorus. • The left lobe of the pancreas is located between the stomach and transverse colon and medial to the splenic head. It may be seen cranial to the gastric fundus and caudal to the left liver from the left of the patient caudal to the ribs. It is often difficult to identify these parts of the pancreas, especially in normal dogs (Hecht and Henry 2007). • It should be noted that gas within the GI tract may hamper evaluation of the pancreas. • The pancratic body and left limb should not exceed 1 cm in width (8.5 mm and 9.5 mm, respectively) in the cat, regardless of age, whereas the left pancreatic duct should not exceed 2.5 mm (Larson et al. 2005). Excessive probe pressure may displace the duodenum, affecting its normal anatomical orientation to the right kidney. Remember that the normal pancreas may not be visible because it is often isoechoic (similar) to the surrounding mesenteric fat. Figure 12.2. Normal pancreas. (A) Normal right pancreatic limb in the sagittal plane in a dog (boundaries identified by the crosses, +). Note the tubular hypoechoic structure within the midpancreatic parenchyma ( arrow). Color flow Doppler can aid in differentiating whether this structure is vessel (pancreaticoduodenal artery or vein) or pancreatic duct. (B) Right pancreatic limb in the sagittal plane in a cat. The pancreas is typically isoechoic to the surrounding mesentery ( asterisk). In the authors’ experience, the echogenicity of the pancreatic parenchyma can vary in normal animals without clinical signs or laboratory evi- dence of pancreatitis. The pancreas can range in echogenicity from mildly hypoechoic to mildly hyperechoic to the surround- ing mesentery, but is typically isoechoic to the surrounding mesentery in the normal state. Pancreatic echogenicity is especially dependent on gain and acoustic output settings. Decreasing the gain settings can aid in pancreatic identification. Serosal margins of the pancreas are typically hyperreflective and can be used to identify the organ’s boundaries. Identification of the descend- ing duodenum along the right dorsolateral aspect of the patient while fanning and scanning medially and laterally along the length of the descending duodenum will aid in identification of the right limb. The sonographer can then follow the right limb to the body of the pancreas. To identify the left limb of the pancreas, the sonographer can begin scanning and fanning in the sagittal plane along the left lateral cranial abdominal wall at the level of the last rib. Here, the gastric fundus and spleen can be easily identified and the sonographer can move caudally along the medial and lateral aspects of the spleen to the cranial pole of the left kidney in search of the organ. Pearl: Remember that the normal pancreas may not be visible because it is often isoechoic to the sur - rounding mesenteric fat and it is a small structure (i.e., well under 1 cm in width). However, the find - ings of moderately hyperechoic (bright white) peri- pancreatic fat and peritoneal fluid adjacent to an enlarged hypoechoic pancreas should prompt a sus- picion of pancreatitis.

Failure to detect evidence of pancreatitis during the POCUS GIT and pancreas examination does not rule out acute pancreatitis, and further testing should be pursued if the history and other clinical findings support a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. 255: 232 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER POCUS GIT and Pancreas Findings and Their Significance Small Bowel To be able to identify intestinal lesions, it is important to gain familiarity with the normal ultrasonographic appearance of the bowel. • In adults, the normal small intestine typically has five ultrasonographicaly identifiable layers, which tend to resemble a “hamburger” on cross‐section (Figures 12.4, 12.5; see also Figure 16.9). • The five layers from the lumen to the serosal surface include the hyperechoic luminal–mucosal gas interface, hypoechoic mucosa, hyperechoic submucosa, hypoechoic muscular layer, and hyperechoic subserosa and serosa. • When thinking of the ultrasonographic layers of the GI tract, the mnemonic “the sun is bright and it’s dark at midnight” may be helpful in remembering that layers starting with an “s,” like the sun, are bright (submucosa and serosa are hyperechoic), while layers starting with an “m,” like midnight, are dark (mucosa and muscular layer are hypoechoic) on the ultrasound image. 256: 233 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS Foreign Bodies The acoustic appearance of GI foreign bodies detected ultrasonographically varies depending on their physical properties. The margins of foreign objects that allow sound to pass through them can be visualized within the GI lumen whereas objects that reflect or attenuate sound often have a hyperechoic interface and produce shadowing beyond their superficial sur - face (Figures 12.6 and 12.7) (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Sharma et al. 2011). • The majority of ultrasonographically detectable GI foreign bodies typically involve a well‐defined hyperechoic, hyperreflective acoustic interface with strong distal acoustic shadowing (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • This is in contrast to intraluminal gas, which tends to result in reverberation artifact (Figures 12.8 and 12.9; see also Figures 16.9–16.13) (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Tyrrell and Beck 2006; Sharma et al. 2011). However, there is some overlap in the shad- owing seen with foreign bodies and intraluminal gas that may render the identification of a foreign body difficult (Tidwell and Penninck 1992). • The acoustic shadowing of foreign bodies may be masked by air, but manipulation of bowel with the probe and changes in patient position can aid evaluation. • Dilation of the intestine orad to a distally shad - owing structure that has a hyperechoic interface between the mucosa and lumen lends support to the presence of intestinal obstruction and suggests the need for surgical exploration (Garcia et al. 2011). • GI foreign bodies should be considered and ruled out when ultrasonographic findings suggest mechanical obstruction or GI irritation. • In the face of appropriate history and physical examination findings, the ultrasonographic detec - tion of peritoneal effusion, gas distension, and abnormal motility (particularly hyperperistalsis with failure to advance intraluminal contents) war- rants a careful search of the GIT for foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Sharma et al. 2011). Linear Foreign Bodies Linear foreign bodies often appear as persistent echogenic or hyperechoic linear structures within the center of plicated small intestinal loops that do not move with peristalsis and remain static throughout the examination (Figures 12.10 and 12.11; see also Figures 16.9–16.13). • The finding of bowel plication is strongly sugges - tive of a linear foreign body and should prompt careful evaluation of the intestine (longitudinal and transverse images) at sites where plication is seen (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • Intestinal corrugation has also been associated with linear foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) but is less specific than plication. Care should be taken to avoid mistaking bowel plication for corrugation (a sign of spasticity and inflamma - tion/enteritis which may be seen with toxins, pri - mary enteropathy or underlying infectious causes) (Figure 12.12) (see later). 257: 234 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Intestinal Obstruction The ultrasonographic diagnosis of intestinal obstruc - tion may be indirect based on the presence of a combined segmental luminal (fluid) distension, hyper- motility in the absence of luminal content progression (Ogata et al. 1996; Manczur et al. 1998), nonuniform intestinal peristalsis and the presence of hyper‐ and hypomotility in the same animal (Schmutz et al. 1997; Manczur et al. 1998). • Patients with these ultrasonographic findings should be carefully evaluated for luminal foreign bodies, intussusception, or even obstructive neo - plasia as their presence further supports a diag - nosis of intestinal obstruction (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Penninck 2008a; Garcia et al. 2011). • The ultrasonographic presence of any two of the above findings has a reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity 98.5% for the diagnosis of intestinal obstruction in cats and dogs (Garcia et al. 2011). However, the presence of only intestinal hyper‐ or hypomotility and concurrent segmental intestinal dilation without progression of luminal content may result in a false‐positive diagnosis of intestinal obstruction (Garcia et al. 2011). Thus, it is impera - tive to continue to search for the presence of foreign bodies, intussusception or mass lesions that would further support mechanical obstruction and sur - gical decision making. Thus, knowing when the animal last ate is important when interpreting GI motility. If possible, GI motility should be assessed within six hours of ingesting a meal (Sanderson et al. 2017). • Caution should be exercised when diagnosing hypomotility based on the presence of food within the GI tract, as food can be ultrasonographically detected in the GI lumen of healthy dogs following 24 hours of fasting. However, the absence of GI contraction in the presence of food supports a diag- nosis of ileus (Sanderson et al. 2017). • Normal contractility varies depending on the sec - tion of GIT evaluated. The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the stomach and proximal duodenum is 4–5 contractions per minute. The number of contractions of the small intestine in the midabdomen is more variable and ranges from one to six contractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989; Sanderson et al. 2017). • Certain GI disorders are associated with changes in intestinal motility, including mechanical bowel obstruction, gastric ulcers, severe pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and neoplastic processes (Garcia et al. 2011). Functional ileus, dur- ing which the lumen of the bowel remains patent, may also be caused by pain, metabolic dister - bances, poor perfusion, and sedative agents (Sanderson et al. 2017). • A generalized decrease in GI motility is reported in small animals with functional and chronic mechanical ileus, whereas a generalized increase in motility is most commonly reported in cases of acute mechanical obstruction (Penninck 2008a). • There is considerable overlap in motility changes between dogs that do and do not have small intestinal obstruction. Changes in motility alone do not indicate the need for surgery (Sharma et al. 2011; Garcia et al. 2011). • If the emergency clinician notes increased or decreased GI motility in a patient with clinical signs of GI disease, further diagnostics (abdominal radiographs or complete abdominal ultrasound examination) should be considered as several sur - gical conditions (foreign bodies, intussusception, and neoplasia) are frequently associated with altered GI motility (Penninck 2008a; Garcia et al. 2011). A thorough evaluation of the GI tract to rule out these conditions is warranted. Decreased intestinal motility due to functional ileus is commonly seen in postoperative patients. • This condition results in a transient cessation of coordinated propulsive motility, most commonly following abdominal surgery (Koscienly and Kalff 2011). • In people, it is associated with abdominal disten - sion, nausea, vomiting, and the inability to pass stools or tolerate a solid diet. 263: 240 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • In addition to the discomfort reported in people, postoperative ileus may predispose patients to wound dehiscence, intussusception, and pulmonary and thromboembolic complications (van Bree et al. 2012). • Several predispositions are associated with acute ileus following postoperative abdominal surgery in people, including intestinal handling during surgery, anesthetic agents, and opioid analgesics (Kehlet 2008; van Bree et al. 2012). • Many small animals are routinely fasted pre‐ and postoperatively, which can also contribute to ileus (Sanderson et al. 2017). Unless otherwise contraindicated, food should be reintroduced to patients as soon as possible following surgical procedures. • If the impression of ileus is due to fasting, reintro- ducing solid food within 24 hours of fasting should promote GI motility (Sanderson et al. 2017). However, if reintroduction of solid food fails to stimulate motility in the patient that has been fasted for less than 24 hours, other causes of functional ileus should be considered. It is currently unknown if liquid diets have the same effect on GI motility as solid diets following a period of fasting. • Long‐term ileus following abdominal surgery is believed to result from inflammation of the intestinal muscularis externa (Kalff et al. 1999). • Postoperative ileus involving the entire gastroin- testinal tract can occur even if only part of the intestine had been handled or is inflamed (van Bree et al. 2012). • If postoperative ileus is noted, measures should be taken to ascertain the underlying cause (opioids, postoperative surgery, abdominal pain, electrolyte imbalances, and peritonitis). • Therapeutic interventions should be implemented and include feeding soon after surgery, early ambulation, epidural analgesia (decreases the need for systemic opioid analgesia which is often associ- ated with ileus), nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents, and minimally invasive surgery (Behm and Stollman 2003; van Bree et al. 2012). Corrugated Intestine Although not always easy to do, it is important to differ- entiate corrugated bowel from plicated bowel as the two pathologies have different etiologies. • Plicated bowel. Plicated bowel is usually associated with intestinal linear foreign bodies that cause the small intestine to bunch around a linear object, resulting in an asymmetrical intestinal pattern (see Figures 12.10, 12.11, 16.9–16.13). The loop of small intestine may weave as it cinches together and con- tracts around the linear foreign body. The finding of plicated bowel may indicate the need for sur - gery, even if the linear foreign body is not ultraso- nographically detected (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) (see Figures 12.9, 12.11, 16.9–16.13). • Corrugated bowel. In contrast, corrugated bowel is a very nonspecific ultrasonographic finding that sug- gests intestinal dysfunction or inflammation, which could result from several different causes (perito- nitis, enteritis, pancreatitis and pancreatic neoplasia, diffuse abdominal neoplasia, enteritis, thrombosis/ infarction, protein‐losing enteropathy, and acute renal failure) (Moon et al. 2003) (see Figure 12.9). • Corrugated intestine. Corrugated intestine occurs secondary to abnormal spastic peristalsis of the bowel resulting in an abnormal wavy (corrugated) pattern to the wall (Moon et al. 2003). The overall direction of the intestine (and serosal margin) tends to appear straight, in contrast to bunched or weaved with pli- cated bowel (see Figures 12.9, 12.12, 16.9–16.13). • Both conditions are most apparent in the sagittal (longitudinal) plane of the small intestine and may be evident in a single loop or sporadically throughout the scan in several loops. • If corrugated bowel is noted in the unstable patient, a POCUS examination of the pancreas and a search for peritoneal fluid using AFAST is warranted as the condition is commonly associated with pancre- atitis and peritonitis. Pancreatitis is particularly common when corrugation of the duodenum is noted (Moon et al. 2003). • If POCUS of the pancreas and/or AFAST examination are unremarkable, or if the patient is stable, a complete abdominal ultrasound exam (or other diagnostic tests) may be indicated to search for other pathol - ogies associated with corrugated bowel, including enteritis (parvovirus, inflammatory bowel disease, lymphocytic plasmacytic enteritis), pancreatic neo- plasia, diffuse abdominal neoplasia, thrombosis/ infarction, protein‐losing enteropathy, and acute renal failure (Moon et al. 2003). Pearl: In differentiating corrugated from plicated bowel, overall direction of the intestine tends to appear straight with corrugated bowel (as with enter- itis or pancreatitis). In contrast, the serosal margin follows the contour of the bunching with plicated bowel (as with surgically indicated linear foreign body) (see Figures 12.10, 12.11, 12.12, 16.9–16.13).
264: 241 POCUS: G ASTROINTESTINAL T RACT AND P ANCREAS Pancreatitis Acute pancreatitis is generally a clinical diagnosis sup- ported by history and physical examination findings. If suspected, a POCUS pancreas examination may further support the diagnosis of pancreatitis. However, ultrasonographic findings may be inconsistent and may not reliably produce sufficient pancreatic paren - chymal change. • A normal ultrasonographic finding does not rule out pancreatitis. • Ultrasound has limited sensitivity (68%) for the detection of pancreatitis, even in severe acute cases (Hess et al. 1998). • Evidence of acute pancreatitis includes an enlarged and diffusely hypoechoic pancreas (Figure 12.17) (Lamb and Simpson 1995; Hecht and Henry 2007). • Variable amounts of peritoneal effusion may be present, and may be amenable to sampling for cytological evaluation. • Surrounding mesenteric fat often appears hyper - choic (bright) due to inflammation, necrosis, and saponification (see Figure 12.17) (Hecht and Henry 2007; Penninck 2008b). • Corrugation of the duodenum or jejunum, and focal pain at the scan site may be present (Hecht and Henry 2007). • Extrahepatic biliary obstruction may accompany pancreatits with bile duct and gallbladder disten - sion. These findings in patients with appropriate history and clinical findings warrant the initiation of therapy for acute pancreatitis. One disadvantage to a POCUS pancreas examination is that the entire bil- iary and pancreatic ductal system requires a greater time commitment and skill level that is typically beyond that of the nonradiologist veterinarian. • If the preliminary POCUS pancreas examination is negative, a complete abdominal ultrasound may be warranted. • When suspected or diagnosed, recheck of the pancreas in 1–3 days should be considered as ultrasonographic signs may become evident with time. Further, follow‐up evaluation will aid in monitoring response to treatment and progres - sion or resolution of changes. Peritoneal Effusion See Chapters 6 and 7. Gas artifacts may be difficult to distinguish from the shadowing associated with some GI foreign bodies. • The stomach is easy to identify due to the presence of rugal folds, but can be difficult to completely image due to luminal ingesta and gas. Luminal contents, or lack thereof, can also affect wall measurements. For example, an empty stomach may give the impression of having a thickened wall. • In dogs, the descending duodenal wall is thicker than other small intestinal segments and can normally measure up to 6 mm in large‐breed dogs. For the remainder of the small bowel, greater than 5 mm (4 mm for the ileum) in dogs and 2.5 mm in cats would generally be considered as thickened (Penninck et al. 1989; Newell et al. 1999). • In cats, the ileum is identified by its bright submu- cosal layer. • The colon can often be differentiated from the small intestinal wall by its thinner wall and lack of motility in normal instances. • Using an acoustic window such as the spleen can enhance imaging of the intestine. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb Gastrointestinal T ract • Normal stomach wall thickness. Dogs 3–5 mm (higher in some giant breeds); cats 2 mm interrugal (up to 4.4 mm if rugal fold is measured) (Nyland et al. 2002). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • Duodenal wall thickness. In dogs, the descending duodenal wall is thicker than other small intestinal segments and can normally measure up to 5 mm in large‐breed dogs (Newell et al. 1999). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosoluminal surface. • Small intestinal measurements. Small bowel wall measurements, other than the duodenum, of greater than 4 mm in dogs and 2.5 mm in cats would gener- ally be considered as abnormally thickened (Newell et al. 1999). Measure from the hyperechoic outer serosal margin to the inner hyperechoic mucosolu- minal surface. • Remembering the five layers of the small intestine. Use the mnemonic “the sun is bright and it’s dark at midnight” to remember that on the US image, layers starting with an “s” like the sun are bright (submu- cosa and serosa are hyperechoic [bright]), while layers starting with an “m” like midnight are dark (mucosa and muscular layer are hypoechoic [dark]). • Direct evidence of GIT foreign bodies. The majority of ultrasonographically detectable GIT foreign bodies typically involve a well‐defined hyperechoic, hyperreflective acoustic interface with strong distal acoustic shadowing (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). • Linear GIT foreign bodies: plication versus corrugation. The finding of bowel plication is strongly sugges- tive of a linear foreign body and should prompt careful evaluation of the intestine (longitudinal and transverse images) at sites where plication is seen (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Garcia et al. 2011). Intestinal corrugation has also been associ- ated with linear foreign bodies (Tidwell and Penninck 1992) but is less specific than plication. • Corrguated versus plicated. In differentiating corru- gated from plicated bowel, overall direction of the intestine tends to appear straight with corrugated bowel (medical causes – enteritis/pancreatitis) in contrast to bunched or weaved with plicated bowel (surgical causes – linear foreign body) (Tidwell and Penninck 1992; Moon et al. 2003). • Indirect evidence of obstruction. Suspect obstruction with the finding of a severely dilated jejunum with luminal dilation measuring greater than 1.5 cm, which may highlight the need for a more extensive and complete abdominal ultrasonographic evalua- tion, abdominal radiographs or exploratory sur - gery. Measure from serosal to serosal surface. • Normal peristalsis – counting contractions. Determine the number of contractions per minute by recording the number of contractions over a three‐minute time period and average to get the number of con- tractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989). ◦ The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the stomach and proximal duodenum is 4–5 contractions per minute. ◦ The mean number of peristaltic contractions of the jejunum averages 1–3 contractions per minute. ◦ The mean number of peristaltic contractions in other areas of small intestine is variable and ranges from one to six contractions per minute (Penninck et al. 1989; Sanderson et al. 2017). ◦ The large bowel (colon) normally has no peristalsis.

276: 253 POCUS: REPRODUCTIVE – MALE however, the immunocompromised individual, children, and pregnant women are considered to be at higher risk and should avoid exposure (Johnston et al. 2001a,b). Care must be taken to protect oneself and other members of the healthcare team by following standard procedures such as wearing exam gloves and avoiding contact with or aerosolization of body fluids. Proper disinfection of surfaces and equipment is mandatory. Rapid slide agglutination tests (RSAT) are available for quick screening tests and agar gel immu - nodiffusion (AGID) can be used to confirm suspected cases. Serological tests have their limitations as B. canis evokes little humoral response. Recent advances in molecular biology have yielded PCR tests but are not yet widely available. A positive identification of the causative organism from blood culture is the definitive proof for brucellosis (Hollett 2010). T esticular T orsion Testicular torsion is more appropriately termed torsion of the spermatic cord. Dogs will typically present with signs of an acute abdomen including abdominal pain, vomiting, dysuria, hematuria, pyrexia, anorexia, leth - argy, or stiff gait. Other physical examination findings may be related to concurrent testicular neoplasia such as truncal, symmetrical alopecia or a pendulous pre - puce seen with Sertoli cell tumors. Ultrasonographic appearance: the testicle of the affected cord is typically enlarged and has a uniform hypoecho- genicity. There may or may not be fluid associated with the epididymis. Absence of blood flow when interro - gated with color flow or power Doppler imaging is the most supportive sign ultrasonographically; definitive diagnosis is made at the time of surgery which is the treatment of choice (Johnston et al. 2001b). T esticular T umors Testicular neoplasia is the most common tumor type in male dogs, second only to skin tumors. Tumors may be unilateral or bilateral and different tumors may be present within the same testicle. The three most common types of tumor are Sertoli cell tumor, seminoma, and interstitial (Leydig) cell tumors. Dogs with testicular neoplasia commonly present with testicular enlargement as the only sign; however, dogs with Sertoli cell tumor may present with bone marrow toxicity (anemia), symmetrical truncal hair loss, and male feminization due to excessive estrogen produc - tion (Johnston et al. 2001b). Testicular tumors may appear as focal masses of varying degrees of distinc - tion from surrounding parenchyma with varying degrees of echogenicity (Davidson and Baker 2009). Ultrasonographic appearance is not specific for tumor cell type and cannot differentiate between benign and malignant conditions (Feeney and Johnston 2007). The Global FAST approach may be used for staging (see Chapter 36). Miscellaneous Scrotal Swellings • Hernias: herniation of small bowel into the scrotum may be detected by finding the normal bowel layers adjacent to the testes; intestinal peristalsis may also be present, helping with the ultrasono - graphic diagnosis (see additionally Chapter 34) (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). • Hematomas, abscesses, and sperm granulomas: may all appear similar to other extratesticular pathology. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say Given the external location and relatively simple anatomy, the testicles are easy to image. Still, make sure to systematically evaluate the three main areas. • Scrotal space – evaluate for fluid, intestines (as in the case of inguinal hernia) or other extratesticular structures, and position of the testicle based upon the epididymis (head caudal, body dorsal, tail dorsocranial). • Testicular parenchyma – evaluate for symmetry in size and shape, tumors, overall echogenicity. • Epididymis – evaluate for focal or diffuse swelling, position (see above), surrounding fluid. Remember, a scrotum that does not contain testicles is not always synonymous with castration; do not forget about cryptorchidism. The prostate is slightly more challenging to image than the testicles, but use the proximal urethra as a guide to lead you directly to it. Evaluate for changes in symmetry and echogenicity in transverse planes. Thoroughly image all edges as paraprostatic pathology can extend well beyond the expected prostatic location. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb Given the large variation in size of dogs between breeds, there are no objective measurements to apply across our patients. Symmetry, rather, is the best rule of thumb. The testicles should be ultrasonographically symmetrical to each other, and the prostate should be ultrasonographi- cally symmetrical about its median plane. In general, the prostate in the castrated dog appears as a smooth, homogeneous swelling around the proximal urethra, with total width being approxi- mately 3–4 times the width of the urethra. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 255 Introduction In the grand scheme of things, reproductive ultraso- nography probably gets the short end of the stick since most of our patients lack their reproductive organs (testicles, ovaries, and uterus) through surgical sterili- zation. However, one should not assume that reproduc- tive sterilization has taken place simply because the altered pet is more common. It is very important to confirm reproductive status since many adopted dogs and cats have unknown medical histories. For instance, a pet owner may assume their female is spayed when in reality she may have never been observed to go into heat. When sexual status is questionable, the shaving of hair and evaluation for surgical spay and neutering scars is helpful, as are other physical examination find- ings such as the lack of mammary development in an older female dog or cat. With ultrasound, most of the reproductive tract may be imaged. In females, this includes the ovaries, uterus, cervix, and mammary glands, and for males, the prostate, scrotum, and testes (see Chapter 13). Of these struc- tures, the uterus makes up the vast majority of POCUS reproductive – female examinations. However, other important conditions of the female and male reproduc- tive tracts are discussed in this chapter and Chapter 13. What the POCUS Reproductive – Female Can Do • Diagnose pregnancy. • Aid in the diagnosis of pyometra, mucometra, and hydrometra. • Aid in the diagnosis of pseudopregnancy. • Aid in the medical management of pyometra. What the POCUS Reproductive – Female Cannot Do • Cannot definitively differentiate pyometra from mucometra and hydrometra. • Cannot provide an accurate fetal count. • Cannot fully screen for intraabdominal free fluid. Indications • Any ill intact female cat or dog to rule out pyometra. • Acute abdomen, especially in intact females with abdominal pain. POCUS: Reproductive – Female Robert M. Fulton CHAPTER FOURTEEN Pearl: In many areas throughout the United States, dogs and cats sterilized in shelters are tattooed either within or adjacent to their surgical site. A ¼–½ inch lime green linear tattoo is commonplace (Figure 14.1). Cats may also have a partial amputation of their left ear tip identifying them as sterilized. Note: An AFAST and the assignment of an abdom- inal fluid score should be minimally performed to screen for any effusions or other obvious AFAST target organ pathology. The Global FAST approach provides even more information regarding the thorax (TFAST), including heart (TFAST) and lung (Vet BLUE), as a quick assessment test for localized versus disseminated disease and comorbidities and complications.

Objectives • Be able to image the basic features of the female reproductive tract. • Identify common ultrasonographic reproductive pathology of the female. • Diagnose pregnancy. Reproductive Conditions of the Female Female reproductive anatomy is shown in Figure 14.2. The major structure involved in most concerning conditions of the bitch or queen is the uterus, and two of its major problems are pyometra and dystocia. Fortunately, the enlarged uterus is very accessible with ultrasound and recognizable by the novice sonogra - pher with minimal training. These conditions and other less common uterine and mammary conditions will be discussed but dystocia is covered in a separate chapter (see Chapter 15). Patient Positioning and Probe Selection Patients are best evaluated in dorsal recumbency with a curvilinear probe and a urine‐filled bladder; how - ever, lateral recumbency and standing position may also be used. Depending on the ultrasound machine, use a medium or comparable abdominal preset. Primarily focusing on longitudinal orientation rather than transverse orientation is usually easier when beginning because the female anatomy is more recognizable. However, performing the POCUS Reproductive – Female examination in standing may be less stressful for some patients. Imaging the Normal Ovary The ovaries lie just caudal to the kidneys. To image the kidneys, start in longitudinal orientation and visualize the ipsilateral kidney. Slide the probe caudally and then fan through this area immediately behind the kidney (Figure 14.3). The normal ovary is often diffi - cult to visualize as it is nearly isoechoic to surrounding tissues but will usually have a subtle cystic appearance (Figure 14.4). For this reason, a linear probe providing greater detail may be useful, especially in small dogs and cats. In large dogs, linear probes may not be able to image deep enough. Overlying gas from small intestine and large bowel can interfere with imaging in this area. Figure 14.1. Spay tattoo. Lime green tattoo scar indi - cating this female dog has been spayed. 280: 257 POCUS: R EPRODUCTIVE – F EMALE Ovarian disease is uncommon in the dog and cat and the reader is referred to additional texts regarding ovarian pathology. Most ovarian disease is associated with changes in size (larger) and echogenicity (often hyperechoic), or cystic change (single or multiple anechoic structures) and is at least screened for using the POCUS reproductive – female examination. Imaging the Normal Uterus Begin the examination with the animal in dorsal recumbency. Keep in mind the normal caudal abdom- inal anatomy. The female reproductive tract lies in bet- ween the urinary bladder and colon (Figure 14.5) (Feeney and Johnston 2007). However, performing the POCUS reproductive – female examination in standing (or lateral recumbency) may be less stressful for some patients. • Place the ultrasound probe in longitudinal orienta- tion just cranial to the pubis where you would expect to find the urinary bladder. • Direct by rocking and sliding the probe caudally to the trigone of the bladder, fanning longitudinally and following urine (normally anechoic [black]) until it triangulates and narrows into the urethra. 282: 259 POCUS: R EPRODUCTIVE – F EMALE • Approximately one‐third of the way along the urinary bladder, depending on bladder size, the uterine body will bifurcate into its two horns. • Follow the uterine horns cranially as they make their way caudal to the kidneys, using combinations of longitudinal and transverse views. This can be chal- lenging given the many twists and turns the uterine horns can make. If you are having problems tracing nongravid, nonfluid‐filled uterine horns, then they are probably not clinically relevant. Although rare, some females may have abnormalities of the tubular reproductive tract such as uterine atresia (not formed), more common in cats. Atresia may involve both or only one uterine horn (Johnston et al. 2001b). Cystic Endometrial Hyperplasia‐Pyometra Cystic endometrial hyperplasia (CEH)‐pyometra com- plex is the most common and important uterine dis - order in bitches. CEH‐pyometra occurs during the luteal phase of diestrus although there are some reports of it occurring during anestrus (Verstegen et al. 2008). General classifications of the complex have been sug - gested according to criteria outlined by Dow and DeBosschere. Dow’s classification scheme uses gross pathology findings and histological lesions while DeBosschere’s scheme also uses the degree of inflammatory reaction, fibroblast proliferation, and endometrium to myometrium ratio. Ultrasonography has been shown to be valuable in the diagnosis of CEH‐pyometra and an efficient tool in the identification of more severe disease as described in both Dow’s and DeBosschere’s schemes (Bigliardi et al. 2004). As pyometra should be included in the differential diagnosis for any intact bitch, regardless of the present- ing signs, the focused female reproductive examination for pyometra is indicated for any ill intact female dog or cat and should be considered in combination with AFAST (the Global FAST approach is better). Ultrasound has a higher sensitivity than radiography for deter - mining the presence of uterine enlargement and fluid accumulation (Feeney and Johnston 2007). The ultra - sound scan is similar to that for dystocia with a primary difference of searching for a fluid‐filled uterus rather than a gravid (fetus‐filled) uterus. Pyometra The initial physical examination finding of purulent vaginal discharge should be an immediate trigger for performing an ultrasound examination to determine the presence of pyometra. Conversely, the finding of a fluid‐filled uterus should trigger a more thorough search for purulent vaginal discharge that may be subtle or initially overlooked on physical examination. • Begin the scan in dorsal recumbency. Start over the urinary bladder in longitudinal orientation, moving along the ventral midline from the caudal abdom - inal region to the xiphoid as described with the dys- tocia evaluation. However, performing the POCUS reproductive – female in standing (or lateral recum- bency) may be less stressful for some patients. • Follow the midline evaluation with the lateral to the mammary gland scan on both the left and right sides to help differentiate the fluid‐filled uterus from the urinary bladder and fluid‐distended small bowel. • Careful scanning should be performed along each horn as thoroughly as possible to avoid a false‐neg- ative evaluation for pyometra. The amount and echogenicity of fluid can vary greatly independent of the pyometra being “open” (cervix open, vaginal discharge) or “closed” (cervix closed, no vaginal discharge), although a “closed” pyometra gen- erally leads to a greater degree of fluid distension. Echogenicity of intraluminal fluid in pyometra ranges from anechoic (pure black) to viscous and echogenic (Figure 14.10). In cases with echogenic fluid, its movement may be characterized by slow, swirling patterns (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). 284: 261 POCUS: REPRODUCTIVE – FEMALE One form of segmental uterine pathology that is likely misdiagnosed as CEH‐pyometra has been termed pseudoplacentational endometrial hyperplasia (PEH). First reported in 1914, PEH also occurs during the luteal phase, with the endometrium remodeling in a way that is very similar to the normal histology of the endometrium at normal placentation sites in preg- nancy (Schlafer and Gifford 2008). While histologically different, clinical presentation and management are the same as for CEH‐pyometra. PEH is likely to form approximately two months post estrus compared to the typical two weeks postestrus occurrence more common with CEH‐pyometra. Surgical versus Medical Management The old adage holds true: “Don’t let the sun set on a pyometra.” Often spoken by a surgeon, this does not mean that all cases of pyometra should be immediately addressed with the scalpel. The unstable, compromised, septic patient should be resuscitated before operation. By optimizing patient status for anesthesia through the initiation of appropriate antibiotics, correction of hypo- volemia, hypoglycemia, and acid–base and electrolyte abnormalities, a favorable outcome is more likely. Detailed preoperative management is beyond the scope of this chapter but may be found in other reference materials (Johnston et al. 2001a,b; Traas 2008). While surgery remains the best option for the vast majority of cases, medical management has been shown to be a viable therapeutic option for the valuable breeding bitch (Verstegen et al. 2008). Because of the potent drugs and unfamiliarity with protocols by most general practitioners and emergency and critical care veterinarians, medical management is best referred to a small animal specialist in therio- genology or other veterinarian experienced in repro- ductive work. Stump Pyometra A stump pyometra should always be on the differential of any acute abdomen in a female spayed dog what- ever matter their age and its location would be ana- tomically between the urinary bladder and the colon. Stump pyometra may occur following ovariohyster - ectomy if a portion of the uterine horns or uterine body is not removed and the animal has increased progesterone concentrations. Progestins may come from endogenous sources such as residual ovarian tissue, sex hormone‐secreting adrenal tumors, or exogenous sources such as progestational compounds used to treat dermatitis, or may be potentially absorbed from creams used for treatment of meno- pausal symptoms in women (Howe 2006). Stump pyometra will not occur in a patient that has under - gone ovariectomy as there is no “stump.” The entire uterus is left intact. Common in European nations, the procedure is beginning to gain popularity in the United States. The same concerns for the development of pyometra (endogenous or exogenous progestin exposure) exist for stump pyometra but at least one study of 72 bitches that underwent ovariectomy did not show any incidence of pyometra over a 6–8‐year follow‐up (Howe 2006). The POCUS reproductive –female examination for stump pyometra is identical to that for pyometra but the primary area of interest is the caudal abdomen, specifically the region between the trigone of the bladder and colon. At this location, search for an area of mixed echogenicity indicative of complex mass effect (England et al. 2003; Davidson and Baker 2009). Other local diseases mimicking or causing a stump pyometra include stump granuloma caused by excess residual devitalized uterine body tissue, use of inappropriate suture material, or poor sur - gical asepsis. Additionally, hematoma formation caused by poor surgical technique or a coagulopathy can serve as a nidus for infection. The finding of free fluid suggestive of acute hemorrhage or peritonitis is another indication for the AFAST scan and assign- ing an abdominal fluid score (see Chapters 6 and 7) and the Global FAST is a more thorough examination for staging (see Chapter 36). Free fluid may only be characterized by abdominocentesis and subsequent fluid analysis. If the case is not urgent, that is, does not have a septic abdomen or large bleed, then a complete detailed abdominal ultrasound may be warranted. Uterine Torsion Uterine torsion in the dog and cat is uncommonly reported. However, the ultrasonographic appearance is as expected for pyometra. The diagnosis of uterine torsion is typically made at surgery (Misumi et al. 2000; Chambers et al. 2011). An AFAST and an assigned fluid score help screen for effusions including secondary hemoabdomen, and a Global FAST can assess for Pearl: Always use ultrasound for guided cystocen- tesis for obtaining urine with a suspect pyometra case. Failure to do so may result in inadvertent aspi- ration of the pus‐filled uterus and contamination of the abdomen.

Mounting of Postoperative Recently In‐heat Spayed Females In‐heat (estrus) spayed females should be kept away from male dogs for two weeks postoperatively because they remain receptive to interested males. Mounting postoperatively can lead to trauma and rupture of the surgical site and insemination of the peritoneal cavity, leading to potentially life‐threat - ening sterile or septic peritonitis (Morley 2006). AFAST and fluid scoring would be the scan best suited to determining whether obvious peritonitis exists (evidence of free fluid), with subsequent char - acterization of ascites by abdominocentesis. Pseudopregnancy All bitches experience the same progesterone profile whether they become pregnant or not. As the proges - terone falls at the end of diestrus, some bitches will expe- rience overt signs of imminent whelping with fully developed mammary glands and milk letdown, nesting behavior, and even abdominal contractions (Johnston et al. 2001c). Although rare, the queen may also show signs of pseudopregnancy. The owners may be convinced their female dog has not been bred but we are all aware of unsupervised receptive females left in the backyard becoming pregnant. A POCUS reproductive – female examination will reliably confirm or refute the presence or absence of fetuses during midgestation and later. Pregnancy Diagnosis Pregnancy is ultrasonographically characterized by segmental fluid distension of the uterine horns. The hallmark is the fetal structures with the segments of fluid (Figure 14.11). These segments are the fetal vesicles. Fetal heart rate can typically be detected ultrasonographically after day 21 post luteinizing hormone (LH) surge. A more thorough discussion of fetal development can be found in Chapter 15. Mammary Glands Due to its superficial location and small thickness, the mammary gland is best imaged with a high‐frequency linear probe. However, if using a curvilinear probe, use the highest frequency available. The normal developed mammary gland at parturition is of a homogeneous appearance. The larger blood vessels may be noted entering the gland. With disease such as mastitis and neoplasia, there is loss of the homogeneous appear - ance (Mattoon and Nyland 2002). The ultrasonographic appearance of mammary gland neoplasia can be quite variable depending on its severity. Small mammary tumors may appear as poorly defined hypoechoic structures with acoustic enhancement artifact, and larger tumors may appear hyperechoic, sometimes with the presence of cysts (Figure 14.12). The spread of tumor tissue among the mammary glands can be successfully detected by ultrasound, and it is very sensitive for detecting such lesions of the mammary gland. 286: 263 POCUS: R EPRODUCTIVE – F EMALE can also be successfully scrutinized for abnormal changes. Ultrasound, however, cannot determine whether lymphadenopathy is due to metastatic spread of tumor tissue or inflammatory reaction (Zuki and Boyd 2004). Pearls, Pitfalls, The Final Say The POCUS reproductive – female examination can lend insight to many disorders such as pyometra, hydrome- tra, and mucometra. Because these diseases are charac- terized by fluid, ultrasound is a sensitive imaging modality for these conditions. Be careful not to confuse the urinary bladder or fluid‐filled gastrointestinal tract (as with small bowel obstruction or severe diarrhea dis- tending the colon) with a diseased uterus. Similar evalu- ation of the uterus can help diagnose pregnancy and ultrasound is a fast, noninvasive method to do so. Quick Reference of Normals and Rules of Thumb • In anestrus, there is no uterine luminal fluid in nor- malcy; however, in estrus there may be a thin echo- genic stripe also considered as a normal finding (Mattoon and Nyland 2002; Verstegen et al. 2008). • The nongravid uterus is tubular, homogeneous in echotexture, with a lumen that is not readily seen and is differentiated from small intestine by lack of peristalsis and intraluminal gas, and absence of the layered appearance characteristics (Mattoon and Nyland 2015). Uterine width varies from 3 to 5 mm in cats and 5 to 10 mm in dogs. • A sonographic hallmark of pyometra is diffuse or segmental fluid dilation of the uterus. • Abdominal radiography is the most accurate way of determining the number of puppies or kittens in the litter (Davidson and Baker 2009). When talking to clients, avoid confirming numbers in the litter using ultrasound because of its inaccuracy. • Normal ultrasonographic layering of the small bowel in the fetus may be used as a guideline for full‐term maturation of puppies and kittens (Mattoon and Nyland 2002) – see Chapter 15. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 265 Introduction Canine and feline dystocia cases are challenging with the clinician having to juggle maternal, fetal, client, and breeder factors. While POCUS dystocia examination cannot help in managing all these elements, it is a valuable tool to gain insight into the fetal side of things and, when combined with the Global FAST approach, the maternal side of things. Assessing fetal development, viability, and fetal stress helps the clinician to make critical decisions in the management of dystocia. What the POCUS Dystocia Can Do • Help assess fetal maturity. • Screen for the presence of fetal stress. • Help manage dystocia by using serial examina- tions for the screening of fetal distress. What the POCUS Dystocia Cannot Do • Cannot provide an accurate fetal count. • Cannot consistently allow the scrutiny of every individual fetus for fetal stress. • Cannot fully screen for intraabdominal free fluid. Indications • Parturition in any dog or cat. • Diagnosed dystocia. • Vaginal discharge during pregnancy. • Green vaginal discharge not followed by passage of a puppy or kitten. Objectives • Discuss final fetal organogenesis. • Discuss fetal heart rate in relation to fetal stress. Dystocia Dystocia: from the Greek dys, meaning difficult, and tokos, meaning birth, or, more simply put, a difficult birthing. More specifically, dystocia is defined as the inability to expel fetuses through the birth canal dur - ing parturition and may result from maternal or fetal factors that prevent delivery from taking place (Jutkowitz 2005). Dogs and cats, like many mammals, tend to undergo parturition during the relative safety of night time. Therefore, dystocia often occurs outside normal business hours for the small animal clinician and becomes the responsibility of the overnight emergency veterinarian. A synergistic relationship between melatonin and oxytocin may, in part, explain this phenomenon (Sharkey et al. 2009). If the clinician presented with a dystocia has been managing the pregnancy from conception, they have a huge body of clinical information that can greatly aid important decision making, particularly in relation to deter - mining if pregnancy is term and parturition is immi- nent. Many times, however, the managing clinician is novel to the pregnancy and must rely on often POCUS: Dystocia Robert M.
