Depth settings that are too low (“too close” to the lung) make it possible to miss lung lesions that fill the screen, and depth set- tings that are too high (“too far away” from the lung) make it possible to miss smaller lung surface pathology (see Chapter 23). Depth may be decreased (magnify) to investigate smaller lung pathology and to view details of the pulmonary–pleural inter- face (PPI), also referred to as the “lung line,” but then should be again increased to the general guide- lines of 4–8 cm (and 9–10 cm for giant breeds) (Figure 22.4). • The focal zone cursor, featured on most ultrasound machines, should be placed at the level of the PPI represented by the hyperechoic line where the vis- ceral and parietal pleura meet in normalcy in the absence of pleural space disease or where the “lung line” is located in pleural space conditions (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3). • Appropriate gain settings are very important. “Overgaining,” making the image too bright (too white), makes it difficult to see the PPI (see Figure 17.10) and artifacts along the lung surface. In gen- eral, the gain setting for Vet BLUE should be less than that for soft tissue during TFAST and AFAST, such that the screen is darker with more contrast. However, gain must also be high enough so that imaging is possible through the far‐field of the screen to accurately identify B‐lines and deeper lesions (see Figure 17.10). • Because the abdominal preset is generally used for the rest of the Global FAST examination, this preset is also often used for Vet BLUE. However, the cardiac preset may provide more contrast and be preferred by some sonographers. The author, how- ever, does the entire Global FAST on the abdom- inal preset and with a single probe type (curvilinear). • The “gator sign” is the same intercostal orientation as for the TFAST CTS view and used for all lung ultrasound orientation (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3). See the Probe Orientation section below. How to Do a Vet BLUE Exam Lung Orientation and the Gator Sign The “gator sign” is an orientation where the probe head is positioned perpendicular to the long axis of the ribs, or in the longitudinal plane for lung. The standard orientation for all lung ultrasound (LUS) begins with the observation of the “gator (alligator) sign” (Figures 22.2 and 22.3). The “gator sign” is created by the rounded rib (alligator’s eyes) with a proximal hyperechoic line in between (alligator’s bridge of nose) creating the image of a partially submerged alligator peering over the water at the sonographer. The space between the rib (alligator’s eyes) is the intercostal region with the hyperechoic line (alligator’s bridge of nose) created by the strong air–soft tissue interface rep- resenting the PPI and the “lung line (surface)” (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3). The author prefers the term “lung line” because when pleural space conditions are present, the integrity of the PPI is lost, and the term “lung line” is more accurate for what is being located and evaluated. The “gator sign” orientation is the starting point for all lung ultrasound (Lisciandro 2011; Lisciandro et al. 2014, 2017; Ward et al. 2017). This orientation is the same as described for the TFAST CTS view (Lisciandro et al. 2008; Lisciandro 2011; Boysen and Lisciandro 2013) (see Figure 17.12). The “gator sign” orientation also allows observation of the to‐and‐fro motion of “lung sliding” (Volpicelli et al. 2012), previously referred to as the “glide sign” in the veterinary litera- ture (see Figure 22.2) (Nyland and Mattoon 2002). “Lung sliding” represents the to‐and‐fro sliding of visceral and parietal pleura during inspiration and expiration, or “lung sliding” along the intercostal space. Its appearance resembles the back‐and‐forth movement of an Etch‐a‐Sketch® cursor (see Figures 22.2 and 22.3) (Lisciandro et al. 2008, 2014a,b; Lisciandro 2011). Probe Orientation: Rotate or Not Some sonographers advocate rotating the probe parallel to the ribs to get another plane of lung during LUS (Figure 22.4). Caution should be exercised unless the sonographer has an extensive knowledge of LUS imaging and its anatomical borders and pitfalls. Rotating the probe and losing sight of the “lung line” can lead to misinterpretations of abdominal structures, dorsal and ventral borders of the pleural cavity Pearl: Consider Vet BLUE as an “extension” from the TFAST CTS view, applied to three additional transthoracic lung regions per hemithorax plus the FAST DH view providing a more comprehensive lung ultrasound examination.

If transverse orientation is attempted, the lung sonogra - pher must always double‐check by appreciating the “gator sign” while rotating the probe from longitudinal to transverse and then returning to longitudinal, the author’s recommended methodology (see Chapter 41). See Confounders of the “Gator Sign” Orientation sec - tion later in this chapter. Thus, the Vet BLUE acoustic windows are referred to as “lung regions.” Naming of the Nine Acoustic Windows There are eight bilaterally applied transthoracic acoustic windows plus the ninth acoustic window as the DH view. • Caudodorsal (Cd) lung region, right and left • Perihilar (Ph) lung region, right and left • Middle (Md) lung region, right and left • Cranial (Cr) lung region, right and left • Diaphragmatico‐hepatic view, single acoustic window Defining the Locations of the Nine Acoustic Windows (Views) T ransthoracic Views Caudodorsal Lung Region (Cd, point 1) This is defined as directly dorsal to the xiphoid in the upper third of the thorax in its 9th–10th intercostal space near the highest point over the pleural cavity with lung. The Cd view starting point is the same acoustic window used for the TFAST CTS. At this region, the sonographer looks for the caudodorsal transition zone (CdTZ) where pleural and abdominal cavities meet because you will move cranial, away from this region to start Vet BLUE. 460: 437 POCUS: V ET BLUE – I NTRODUCTION AND I MAGE A CQUISITION Perihilar Lung Region (Ph, point 2) This is defined as the point in the middle third of the thorax between the 6th and 7th intercostal spaces approximating the perihilar region on a thoracic radiograph. The Ph (point 2) is found by “drawing” a line from the Cd (point 1) to the elbow. This is done with your acoustic coupling medium and your hand by roughing the hair along this “Vet BLUE line.” Halfway from the Cd (point 1) is the Ph (point 2) (Figure 22.11). Middle Lung Region (Md, point 3) This region is defined as the lower half of the thorax over the heart approximating the 4th–5th intercostal spaces. If the heart is in view and obscuring lung, then sweep immediately dorsal in that same intercostal space(s), finding the “lung line” and then performing the Vet BLUE examination (Figure 22.12). Cranial Lung Region (Cr, point 4) This is defined as the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd intercostal spaces – in other words, in the region caudal to the thoracic inlet and cranial to the heart. The foreleg often needs to be gently extended cranially to get this view (see Figure 22.11). The soft tissue and vessels of the thoracic inlet help define the Cr (point 4). Identify the thoracic inlet’s soft tissue structures, the cranial transition zone (CrTZ) (Figure 22.13), and then slide caudally over the first three intercostal spaces. The author recommends always extending the foreleg from the elbow region rather than the paw because some dogs (and cats) do not like their paws touched and become stressed or bite when their paws are handled. 590: 567 POCUS: EYE Actions • Measure IOP , and treat glaucoma if needed. Do not give mydriatics (atropine, tropicamide) if the IOP is high, as this may exacerbate glaucoma. Miotics (latanoprost, pilocarpine) are not specifically con- traindicated and may help to keep the lens trapped in the posterior segment. • Topical antiinflammatories may be needed if there are clinical signs of anterior uveitis. • Based on clinical signs and history, need to deter - mine primary cause as discussed above. The poste- rior location of the lens, alone, does not necessarily require specific treatment but is more an indicator of possibly more significant ocular pathology that must be identified and addressed. Consider referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist. Retinal Detachment Clinical Findings • History: possible acute or subacute vision loss (may not be noticeable to owner if unilateral). • Signalment: variable. • Eye exam: reduced or absent PLR, menace and dazzle; hyphema (blood in anterior chamber); rest- ing mydriasis (in affected eye), especially with aniso- coria; possible retinal hemorrhages or generalized red color from behind pupils; visible retinal detach- ment seen on fundic exam (best seen using indirect ophthalmoscopy, rather than direct ophthalmoscopy (for examination techniques see Cho 2019). Ultrasonographic Findings • If intraocular bleeding is present, this may be visible as echogenic structures (see Intraocular Hemorrhage section below). • The retinal detachment itself is seen as a thin bright continuous curvilinear structure in the posterior segment that can be followed back to the optic nerve head, often making a V‐ or Y‐shape or “gull wing” appearance (Figure 27.18A). • This linear structure is almost always attached at the ora serrata (junction between retina and ciliary body) (Figure 27.18B). • Often accompanied by other echogenic structures (vitreal strands, hemorrhage, asteroid hyalosis) in the posterior segment. • Retinal detachments may be bullous (retina sepa- rated from the posterior eye wall) or “flat” (retina close to the posterior eye wall) (Figure 27.18C). • Retinal detachments may be completely detached (only attached at the optic nerve head and ora serrata) or partial (still attached to the choroid in some areas). • It is possible to see discontinuities (tears or holes) in the detached retina, but not common. • The subretinal space is more often echolucent (indi- cating a serous retinal detachment) than echogenic (indicating subretinal blood, cells or a mass), and is very often more echolucent than either the retina or the posterior eye wall. • The presence of vitreal blood and vitreal mem- branes/degeneration can make identification of a retinal detachment, especially a partial detach- ment, much more difficult (see Figure 27.26). These findings can significantly reduce image contrast, causing a missed diagnosis of detach- ment, or a false positive if vitreal membranes are oriented to masquerade as a detachment (Gallhoefer et al. 2013). • If available, the use of contrast enhancement may improve the ability to differentiate a detached retina from vitreal membranes by identifying vas- cularization within the suspect structure(s), and may be more useful than using Doppler (Labruyère et al. 2011). • Seeing attachment points of a suspected retinal detachment (especially at the optic nerve and ora serrata) greatly increases the chance that a sus- pected detachment is truly a retinal detachment. Sweeping the probe across a suspect area in differ- ent directions will improve your ability to see this. Actions • Measure blood pressure especially if retinal detach- ment is nontraumatic and bilateral; treat systemic hypertension (systolic blood pressure >180 mmHg) if present and consistent with clinical signs. • Look for signs of anterior or posterior uveitis (miosis, aqueous flare, hypotony, iris hyperemia, etc.). If present, and cornea is fluorescein negative, and if patient will not be seen by a veterinary oph- thalmologist within 48–72 hours, begin topical treatment, such as NeoPolyDex drops or ointment, or 1% pred acetate suspension q6–12h, and systemic nonsteroidal antiinflammatories. If patient will be seen immediately, therapy may be delayed until examination. • If hyphema is present, measure IOP , and treat with antiglaucoma medications if IOP >25 mmHg (0.5% timolol q12h and/or 2% dorzolamide q8h, or the combination drop timolol/dorzolamide q8h), +/‐ oral methazolamide 1 mg/lb up to q8–12h). The latter may be difficult to find and can be considered optional.

592: 569 POCUS: E YE Intraocular Masses Clinical Findings • History: variable; many owners are unaware of the eye looking abnormal and the eye is often not pain- ful until either uveitis, glaucoma or hyphema develops; signs referable to these secondary prob - lems are often the presenting complaint. • Signalment: variable, but generally middle‐aged to older animals. • Eye exam: variable but any of the following: deformed globe in advanced cases (outward focal bulging of eye wall); hyphema; focal peripheral corneal edema if mass is touching inside of cornea (Figure 27.19A), dyscoria, iris thickening, presence of a visible mass in either anterior or posterior segment (pigmented or nonpigmented, and espe - cially near eye wall) (Figures 27.20 and 27.21); lens subluxation; focal retinal detachment associated with a solid‐looking structure; any of the above with glaucoma. Ultrasonographic Findings • A bulge in the normally spherical eye wall might be seen in advanced cases, with a mass as described below just under the area of the bulging eye wall. • Hyphema might be seen as indistinct, echogenic material in the anterior chamber. • Dyscoria would be difficult to appreciate on ultra - sound, but an area of iris thickening might be seen if thickening is marked (see Figures 27.19B and 27.20C). • The most common type in dogs (uveal melanoma) usually appears as an attached, rounded, uni - formly echogenic structure in the area of the iris or ciliary body (less commonly the choroid) with a sharp border, possibly slightly pushing the lens off‐ center (see Figure 27.19B,C). • Differentiate masses from uveal cysts, which would be very thin‐walled, echolucent within, and either free‐floating or attached to the posterior iris, pupil margin or ora serrata. • Masses are often broad‐based (on the eye wall) and not pedunculated (see Figure 27.21). Pearl: Retinal reattachment surgery, while not as commonly performed in animals as it is in humans, is increasingly available for animals with primary retinal detachment. Figure 27 .19. (B) A large, uniformly echogenic mass is present in the anterior chamber of the same eye, originating from the iris and slightly pushing the lens to the right side of the image. Note the rounded, relatively distinct border between the mass and the anterior chamber and lens. The lens itself, as well as the vitreous, is otherwise normal and echolucent. Pearl: The prognosis for vision is better if the subreti- nal space is echolucent (transudate) and worse if echogenic (blood, cells, mass). The prognosis also worsens with increasing duration of the detachment. Pearl: If retinal detachment is present and associ - ated with trauma, the prognosis for vision is guarded to poor (Book et al. 2008).

594: 571 POCUS: E YE by a veterinary ophthalmologist immediately, top- ical therapy can be delayed until examination. • Measure IOP; if glaucoma present (IOP >25 mmHg), begin antiglaucoma medications, such as 0.5% timolol q12h, 2% dorzolamide q8h, or dorzolamide/ timolol q8h, if not being seen by an ophthalmologist within 24 hours. Do not give mydriatics (tropicamide, atropine) as this may exacerbate glaucoma. • Most intraocular neoplasms (such as melanoma, ade- noma) are primary and late to metastasize; however, a minimal systemic work‐up with baseline bloodwork, urinalysis, and thoracic radiographs, with or without abdominal imaging (ultrasonography, radiography), is indicated if systemic illness is present since intraoc- ular neoplasia (such as lymphosarcoma, hemangio- sarcoma, etc.) may represent metastatic disease. • Enucleation may ultimately be needed for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. • Consider timely referral to a veterinary ophthal - mologist as necessary for confirmation and defini - tive therapy. Intraocular Hemorrhage Clinical Findings • History: variable; possible vision loss, possible trauma, change in appearance, possible history of coagulopathy. • Signalment: variable. • Eye exam: hyphema (see Figure 27.2A), red or red‐ black haze visible inside eye from behind iris and lens, inability to visualize any fundic details; pupil may be any size and may still be responsive to light. Since the possible causes of intraocular hemorrhage include retinal detachment, posterior segment mass or injury, trauma, systemic hypertension, coagulop- athy and possibly vascular disease, accompanying history and clinical signs vary with the underlying cause. IOP may be low, normal or high. Ultrasonographic Findings • If hyphema is present, diffuse echogenic material will be present in the anterior chamber. • Variably sized and shaped structure(s) within the vitreous with poorly defined borders that are semi‐ mobile (try jiggling the eye) but not completely gravity dependent; can be multifocal; may be densely and uniformly echogenic, anechoic, hypoechoic or heterogeneous; may be composed of multiple point‐like echoes; are often near the eye wall (where the original bleeding occurred) (see Figure 27.26). • Differentiate on ultrasound from asteroid hyalosis, which tends to have a lucent peripheral vitreal border and is generally uniform (Figure 27.22) but both have partial mobility and may also have concurrent vitreal strands. • May be associated with retinal detachment, intraocular masses and scleral rupture (see corresponding sections in this chapter). The presence of echogenic blood in any location could greatly obscure the ultrasonographic visi - bility of both normal structures and actual lesions. • Need to differentiate from a solid intraocular mass, which will not be mobile at all, will always be attached to the eye wall, and will typically have a more distinct interior border than a hemorrhage. Pearl: All the above ophthalmic medications are human drugs, and drops are generally available at human pharmacies. Pearl: In the absence of trauma, two of the most common causes for spontaneous intraocular bleeding in older dogs are retinal detachment and intraocular neoplasia. In cats, neoplasia and hyper - tensive retinopathy with retinal detachment are the most common in the author’s experience. Figure 27 .22. Optic nerve and asteroid hyalosis. Asteroid hyalosis, a common finding in older dogs, is typically seen as an amorphous, fairly uniform, semimobile echogenic material in the normally echolucent vitreous. It is often denser in the center of the vitreous, leaving the more peripheral vitreous echogenic.

596: 573 POCUS: EYE Suspected Retrobulbar Masses/ Exophthalmos Distinguishing between exophthalmos and buphthal- mos is key to choosing the right treatment plan when the eye is “bulging” (see Figure 27.4). Clinical Findings of Exophthalmos (Pushed‐Out Eye) • History: variable, may be acute or gradual onset. • Signalment: variable due to the varying etiologies. • Eye exam: globe protrudes and has reduced retro- pulsion (compare to the other side by palpating gently with an index finger on each closed eye) but is not enlarged in size (see below); globe deviation, not necessarily with strabismus; elevated nictitans; secondary lagophthalmos and central corneal exposure; indentation of sclera may be seen on fundic exam but fundus is otherwise normal; vari- able changes in vision and in IOP – most cases still have intact vision and normal IOP . • Physical exam: also look for possible ipsilateral dental disease or evidence of inflammation in soft palate; pain on opening mouth (variable); local lymphadenopathy; ipsilateral nasal disease; sneez- ing and nasal discharge; palpable periocular/ orbital bony abnormalities. Clinical Findings Supportive of Buphthalmos (Large Eye) • History: gradual or chronic onset. • Signalment: for dogs, a breed predisposed to pri- mary glaucoma, for example any terrier breed, bas- sett hound, cocker, beagle, sharpei, Siberian husky, shih tzu, Dalmatian, Great Dane, etc. For cats, clinical signs and history of chronic or recurrent uveitis. Secondary glaucoma can occur with any age or breed having prior intraocular disease. • Eye exam: enlarged (and not just pushed out) globe; signs of chronic glaucoma including blindness, episcleral injection, diffuse corneal edema, corneal striae, negative PLR, mydriasis, high IOP , hyperreflective tapetum, thin retinal ves- sels, dark and/or cupped optic nerve head. Ultrasonographic Findings of Retrobulbar Mass/ Exophthalmos • Affected globe is normal size. • Globe indentation by the mass may be seen (Figure 27.24B,C). • Mass effect of variable echotexture behind the globe (Figure 27.24B,C). • Variably discrete mass borders. Pearl: Intraocular bleeding is a nonspecific finding. Differentials include systemic disease (systemic hypertension, coagulopathy, vasculitis, etc.), ocular disease (uveitis, retinal detachment, neoplasia, pos- sibly lens luxation, etc)., trauma, etc. Referral is indi- cated unless the cause is definitively identified, treated, and managed. Note: Differentiate exophthalmos from buphthal- mos using ultrasound by measuring globe at widest front‐to‐back diameter and compare to normal eye (normal typically around 19–21 mm) (Figure 27.23). Buphthalmos is only caused by glaucoma, and is thus distinctly different in pathology from exophthalmos. Pearl: Cases of buphthalmos still warrant timely referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist for glau- coma treatment for the affected blind eye and glau- coma prophylaxis for the remaining sighted eye. Pearl: Indentation is more consistent with a mass or cyst rather than cellulitis. Pearl: Echogenicity versus echolucency is often not predictive of the etiology of a retrobulbar mass (Mason et al. 2001). Pearl: Cellulitis/abscesses usually have very indis- tinct borders and variable echogenicity, and oblit- erate/obscure normal structures; cystic structures typically are more sharply marginated with anecho- lucent/anechoic interior; neoplastic masses tend to be more discrete (than cellulitis/abscess) and more uniform, but may have cavitation, indistinct bor - ders, and variable echogenicity and even be occult via ultrasonography (Mason et al. 2001).
597: 574 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • The mass may be attached to or separate from the globe. • Most common differentials include abscesses (gen- erally acute onset and very painful on opening mouth), soft tissue or bony neoplasia (generally gradual onset and of varying degrees of pain – may not be painful at all). • Other less likely differentials include cysts (including sialoceles), foreign bodies, cellulitis or inflammation of retrobulbar tissues (sialoadenitis, extraocular muscle myositis), bony orbital masses, hamartomas, vascular anomalies, parasitic disease. These may be very difficult to distinguish (Welihozkiy et al. 2011). • Bony destruction is more indicative of neoplasia, and is more easily detected using radiography. Actions • If neoplasia is suspected, initiate a work‐up to screen for metastatic disease including baseline bloodwork, urinalysis, skull and thoracic radiog - raphy with or without abdominal imaging (ultra - sonography, radiography); referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist or surgeon may be necessary. • If an orbital abscess is suspected supported by find- ings of pain, ipsilateral soft palate swelling, gross dental disease, leukocytosis, lethargy, +/‐ fever, perform an oral exam and appropriate imaging, such as dental and skull radiographs, with appli - cable dental treatment; if found, oral abscess explo- ration, drainage, cytology, biopsy, and culture as indicated; systemic antibiotics and analgesics; advanced imaging and referral to a veterinary oph- thalmologist, surgeon, or dentist, as per clinical impression may be necessary (Hartley et al. 2007). Fine needle aspiration of suspected retrobulbar masses carries the risk of hemorrhage, possible iatrogenic globe puncture or nerve damage, but is often diagnostic for neoplasia and infection when the needle is appropri - ately placed. Aspiration aided by simultaneous ultra - sound can reduce these risks. Vascular anomalies, although extremely rare, may develop significant bleeding when aspirated or biopsied, and may not be amenable to typical hemorrhage control maneuvers. Most cases of primary orbital/periorbital neoplasia are malignant, for example nasal or third eyelid adeno- carcinoma, soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcoma, squamous cell carcinoma, meningioma, glioma, lym - phoma (Kern 1985; Attali‐Soussay et al. 2001). The marked chemosis and hyperemia of the bulbar conjunctiva and nictitans are due to the protruding globe causing tight compression of the lower lid against the globe. 599: 576 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER (which might be located somewhere behind the front exposed part of the eye and thus not visible externally) (Rampazzo et al. 2006); orbital or skull fractures. Ultrasonographic Findings Extreme care should be used in approaching ocular ultrasonography in these cases, if at all. Avoid any direct contact with the suspected ruptured area; use sterile gel and adequate topical and anesthesia (see above) or the retrobulbar angle for probe placement; avoid any pressure at all to the globe and excessive restraint. • Globe not spherical like normal. • Globe may be smaller than the other eye (compare diameter of each eye). • Eye wall may not be clearly visible in all views – intraocular structures may seem to blend in with adjacent extraocular structures consistently in one location (see Figure 27.26B,C). • Will often be accompanied by sonographic evi - dence of retinal detachment, vitreal hemorrhage, and/or lens luxation or loss (see above corresponding sections). • The interior of the whole globe may appear hetero- geneously echogenic (due to the presence of blood and fibrin) with no discernible normal structures except for the lens, which will remain echolucent against this echogenic background if present. Actions • Evaluate first for life‐threatening trauma such as skull fractures, traumatic brain injury, cavitary hemorrhage, lung contusions, pneumothorax, etc. with a basic trauma work‐up. • Do not aggressively clean off adherent mucus‐like material from the eye surface. This may be fibrin that is actually sealing the defect, and removing it may cause a releak of intraocular contents as well as acute pain. • Administer systemic pain medications, systemic antiinflammatories and analgesics, systemic antibi- otics, and topical ophthalmics (antibiotics, atro - pine; drops preferred, avoid ointments) as dictated by patient. Figure 27 .25. Traumatic globe rupture in a dog. This unfortunate dog had been kicked by a moose, causing major ocular injury. Note that the corneal contour of this left eye is not spherical but rather appears squashed into a flatter shape by the eyelids. This is because the globe has lost its tension and shape due to a large rent at the limbus. Hyphema obscures all the intraocular structures, but a care - fully performed ocular ultrasound (not shown) from behind the orbital ligament might reveal a posterior rent and the presence of a retinal detachment, lens luxation or lens extrusion. Important: In cases of suspected globe rupture, extreme caution should be exercised when considering ocular ultrasonography. Avoid any direct contact with the suspected ruptured area and if ultrasound imaging is necessary (to confirm or clarify clinical suspicion) use only sterile gel after adequate topical anesthesia, or the retrobul - bar view, if at all. Any pressure at all to the globe or resis - tance by the patient may be painful and will cause further eye damage. The patient may be better served by avoiding ultrasound altogether and simply referring to an ophthal - mologist for definitive care. Pearl: Stabilize animal systemically first before working up the eye! Pearl: If the eye is too painful to be imaged with top- ical anesthesia and other clinical signs are sugges - tive of globe rupture, the patient may be better served by avoiding ultrasound altogether due to the potential for causing further damage. Pearl: Stabilize the critical patient before addressing the ocular component. Pearl: The owner’s ability to give topical medica - tions may be limited due to patient pain. Due to the possibility of further injury in the act of topical drug administration, topical medications may not be worth the trouble.
600: 577 POCUS: E YE Figure 27 .26. Globe trauma in an outdoor cat. This 3‐year‐old male Abyssinian sustained unknown trauma while outdoors. Significant subconjunctival hemorrhage and a central corneal rupture were seen, and the entire anterior chamber was full of fibrin, obscuring visibility of iris and posterior structures (A). Ocular ultrasound shows extensive echogenic material with unorganized linear structures mixed with smaller echolucent areas. 601: 578 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER • Very carefully place an E‐collar to prevent self‐trauma. • If a penetrating foreign body is seen, leave it in place if immediate, timely referral is possible; if a foreign body is clearly visible, very mobile and loose enough to fall out on its own before referral to an ophthalmologist is possible, it may be very care- fully removed in the clinic under clean conditions with at least topical anesthesia; however, there is risk of damaging the eye and causing leakage of intraocular contents, allowing for intraocular infec- tion, bleeding, and increased risk of loss of the eye. • Many cases will require enucleation, but referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist may provide options for salvaging the globe and possibly vision. Pearls and Pitfalls, The Final Say • Important to correlate ultrasound findings with clinical ophthalmic signs! Always do a complete ocular examination first when presented with an ocular complaint. • Very helpful to compare the abnormal eye to the other eye as a control, especially when the other eye is unaffected. • Adjust magnification (depth) to a level adequate to distinguish lesions. • Adjust gain both by increasing and decreasing to help distinguish real findings from artifacts. • Unless you are very comfortable with your diag- nosis and treatment plan, it is wise to adhere to the following statement: if an eye is diseased enough to require ultrasound, it should most likely be referred to an ophthalmologist for follow‐up. • Use Global FAST to help determine if the ocular problem is localized or part of disseminated dis- ease. Global FAST surveys the abdomen (AFAST), thorax (TFAST) including heart (TFAST) and lung (Vet BLUE) and also helps assess patient volume status (see Chapters 6, 7, 17, 18, 22, 23, 36, and 37). Published 2021 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lisciandro/ultrasound2 Introduction Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for brain imaging. However, this technique involves high costs such as equipment acquisition and mainte- nance, making it difficult to perform as a routine any- where, especially in veterinary medicine. Moreover, MRI requires some form of chemical restraint, which is commonly inhaled general anesthesia via endotracheal intubation, which carries patient risk. On the other hand, transcranial ultrasonography (TCUS) has the advantage of being noninvasive and low cost, which has great value in the diagnosis of brain disorders such as hydrocephalus, tumors, congenital malformations, and traumatic processes, and can be performed without the need to anesthetize the patient. Transcranial ultrasonography is considered a screen- ing method for neuroimaging examination in many situations. It may be applied to cases of trauma, patients with anesthesia limitations and owners’ eco- nomical restrictions, before patients are imaged by computed tomography (CT) or MRI. In human medicine, TCUS has been compared to CT and MRI in children in order to detect the cause of head- ache. While CT and MRI were able to detect tumors as the primary disease in 3.8% of these cases, TCUS was less effective, detecting tumors as primary disease in 2.2% of cases. However, the low cost, lower patient risk, and convenience through point‐of‐care imaging appli- cations make TCUS an option in clinical practice not only as a screening test but also when measurements and monitoring are needed (Abrão et al. 1998; Wang et al. 2002). In children, the temporal, parietal, and suborbital acoustic windows are commonly utilized when performing TCUS (Wang et al. 2002). These acoustic windows may be used for animals but the breg- matic fontanelle and temporal bone have been most studied as acoustic windows for TCUS in veterinary medicine (Gallagher et al. 1995; Lorigados and Pinto 2013; Cintra et al. 2014). Both human and veterinary protocols additionally use the foramen magnum as an acoustic window to assess the caudal fossa. Despite many published veterinary studies (Hudson et al. 1998; Carvalho et al. 2007; Duque et al. 2009) some neurologists still remain uncomfortable with the potential use of TCUS. However, many small animal patients have suitable transcranial acoustic windows that allow screening for structural lesions with the advantages of being a rapid, safe (no anesthesia requirement and minimal restraint), point‐of‐care, imaging application. One of the main indications for TCUS is ventricular system evaluation. Ventricular measurements may be used clinically and compared to normal published reference values (Table 28.1). What POCUS Brain Can Do • Screen for anatomical abnormalities of the brain. • Screen for structural abnormalities of the brain. • Provide monitoring measurements (ventricular system, focal lesions). What POCUS Brain Cannot Do • Account for variables of skull bone thickness. • Account for anatomical variations between patients and species. • Differentiate between malignant and benign lesions. 603: 580 POINT-OF-CARE ULTRASOUND TECHNIQUES FOR THE SMALL ANIMAL PRACTITIONER Indications • Any small‐breed dog or cat with neurological signs and accessible transcranial acoustic windows. Objectives • Understand how to image the three transcranial acoustic windows. • Appreciate basic ultrasonographic brain anatomy. • Understand the value and limitations of transcra- nial Doppler ultrasound (TCUS). How to do POCUS Brain Probe T ype Real‐time B‐mode TCUS probe requirements are as follows. • Linear probes of 5–10 MHz with depth range of 1.0–4.0 cm for neonates with or without an open rostral fontanelle. • Curvilinear (microconvex) probes of 2–6 MHz with high resolution and depth range of 1.0–6.0 cm for mature small‐breed dogs without an open breg- matic fontanelle. Acoustic Windows for POCUS Brain Three transcranial acoustic windows may be used for POCUS brain: rostral, temporal, and suboccipital. Rostral Acoustic Window The rostral window is used in patients with an open bregmatic fontanelle, including puppies <1–3 months old, kittens <5 months old, and many toy breeds. However, even in a closed bregmatic fontanelle having a thin frontal bone, an acoustic window may be pre- sent because ultrasound can image through thin bone. T emporal and Suboccipital Acoustic Windows The temporal window is located above zygomatic arch, and the suboccipital window should be used in all cases (Figures 28.1, 28.2, 28.3, and 28.4). Ultrasonographic Anatomy The brain is surrounded by the bones of the skull and during fetal development, fibrous sutures appear bet - ween them. These sutures extend to intersections called the fontanelles. Compared to humans, at birth most dogs and cats have either a very small fontanelle (approximately 0.5–3 mm) or one that is completely ossified. The toys and chondrodystrophic breeds are exceptions, in which the fontanelle between the frontal and parietal bones is relatively greater in size and can remain open for up to three months or in some cases remain persistently open throughout life. The contours of the bone can be identified as a hyperechogenic (bright white) arcuate line in the near‐field of the image, with brain parenchyma (gray and white brain matter) appearing with moderate degrees of echogenicity. The encephalon is contained in a cavity inside the skull, whose rostral border is limited by a bony plate, called the ethmoid, and caudally limited by the occipital bone. Laterally, the cavity is limited by the temporal, parietal, and frontal bones. The dome of the cavity (calvaria) is formed by the frontal and parietal bones, and the base is formed by the ethmoid, prephe- noid, and basisphenoid bones. Its most prominent internal anatomical feature is the cerebellar tentorium, which is a large projection at the junction of the dorsal and caudal walls, forming the middle portion of the cerebellum in the transverse fissure of the brain (Hudson et al. 1989; Cartee et al. 1993; Homco 1996). The cerebral hemispheres are divided from each other by a deep longitudinal fissure; the cerebellum is divided by a transverse fissure. Each hemisphere is divided into lobes denominated by the corresponding bone portion that covers them. The frontal lobe is the most rostral portion, limited caudally by the crossed groove. The parietal lobe is caudal to the folded and dorsal groove of the Sylvian gyrus and extends cau - dally to the caudal third of the cerebral hemisphere. The occipital lobe includes the caudal third of the cerebral hemisphere. The temporal lobe consists of the spins and grooves of the ventrolateral portion of the cerebral hemispheres, and part of the Sylvian spins are located in that region (Hudson et al. 1989; Figure 28.7 .
